myth: Eating chicken soup helps soothe a common cold
claim: Chicken soup can help relieve cold symptoms
explanation: The warm broth replaces fluids and essential minerals lost from a cold or a runny nose. The rising steam opens up your nose and throat, while the warm liquid thins mucus.

claim: Using sunscreen can cause cancer
explanation: Sunscreen actually protects against skin cancer by blocking harmful UV rays. There is no scientific evidence that sunscreen causes cancer. Regular sunscreen use is recommended by dermatologists worldwide.

myth: The vaccine is more dangerous than COVID-19 because of side effects
claim: COVID-19 vaccines are more dangerous than the virus itself
explanation: COVID-19 vaccines have been extensively tested and proven safe. While vaccines may have mild side effects, the risk of serious complications from COVID-19 is much higher. Vaccines prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

claim: Childhood vaccines cause autism spectrum disorder
explanation: No evidence links vaccines to autism. The original study claiming a link was discredited and retracted. Large population studies have consistently failed to show a connection.

claim: Vaccine ingredients are dangerous and harmful
explanation: Vaccine ingredients undergo extensive testing before approval. Ingredients are present in extremely small and safe quantities. They help vaccines remain effective, stable, and sterile.

myth: Natural immunity is better than immunity from vaccines
claim: Getting a disease naturally provides better immunity than vaccination
explanation: Contracting diseases naturally can result in severe illness, disability, or death. Vaccines provide immunity without the risks associated with infection. Vaccination is a safer way to build protection.

claim: Breastfeeding provides all the immunity babies need
explanation: Breast milk provides valuable antibodies and immune support. It does not provide protection against all vaccine-preventable diseases. Babies still require routine immunizations according to the vaccination schedule.

myth: Too many vaccines kill our immune system
claim: Multiple vaccines overwhelm and damage the immune system
explanation: The immune system encounters thousands of germs every day. Vaccines expose the body to only a tiny fraction of antigens compared to natural infections. Scientific studies show vaccines do not overwhelm the immune system.

myth: Vaccines remain in your body forever and cause harmful long-term effects
claim: Vaccine components stay in the body indefinitely and cause harm
explanation: Vaccine components are processed and removed by the body over time. Most vaccine ingredients leave the body within days or weeks. Long-term safety monitoring has not shown vaccines remaining indefinitely.

myth: Pregnant people should never be vaccinated
claim: Vaccination is unsafe during pregnancy
explanation: Several vaccines are specifically recommended during pregnancy. Vaccination protects both the pregnant individual and the baby. It reduces the risk of serious complications from vaccine-preventable diseases.

claim: Drinking water can prevent coronavirus infection
explanation: Drinking water is important for overall health. Water does not prevent coronavirus infection. Preventive measures include vaccination, hand hygiene, and respiratory precautions.

claim: Garlic can prevent or protect you from COVID-19
explanation: Garlic is a healthy food with nutritional benefits. WHO found no evidence that garlic prevents COVID-19 infection. Garlic should not replace proven public-health measures.

claim: Alcohol consumption can kill coronavirus in the body
explanation: Alcohol consumption does not kill coronavirus inside the body. Excessive alcohol intake can damage health and weaken the immune response. WHO has specifically debunked this claim.

claim: High temperatures prevent coronavirus transmission
explanation: COVID-19 spread in many countries with hot and humid climates. High temperatures do not prevent coronavirus transmission. Vaccination and infection-control measures remain necessary regardless of the weather.

claim: Snow and cold temperatures eliminate coronavirus
explanation: The virus can spread in both warm and cold climates. Snow and cold temperatures do not eliminate coronavirus. Preventive measures are required regardless of weather conditions.

claim: Mosquitoes can transmit coronavirus
explanation: COVID-19 is primarily spread through respiratory droplets and aerosols. There is no evidence that mosquitoes transmit COVID-19. WHO has explicitly stated that mosquitoes do not spread the virus.

myth: UV radiation can be used safely on skin to kill COVID-19
claim: UV lamps can disinfect hands and skin from coronavirus
explanation: UV radiation can damage the skin and eyes. WHO advises against using UV lamps to disinfect hands or skin. Proper handwashing and alcohol-based sanitizers are safer and more effective.

claim: Antibiotics can prevent coronavirus infection
explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses. COVID-19 is caused by a virus (SARS-CoV-2). Unnecessary antibiotic use contributes to antimicrobial resistance.

claim: Antibiotics can treat viral illnesses like COVID-19
explanation: Antibiotics are effective only against bacterial infections. Viral illnesses such as COVID-19, colds, and influenza cannot be treated with antibiotics. Misuse of antibiotics contributes to global antimicrobial resistance.

myth: Hand dryers are effective in killing the COVID-19 virus
claim: Hot-air hand dryers can kill coronavirus
explanation: Hot-air hand dryers do not kill the coronavirus. Handwashing with soap or using alcohol-based hand rub is effective. Hand dryers should only be used to dry hands after they have been cleaned.

myth: Cow urine prevents or cures COVID-19
claim: Cow urine can prevent or treat coronavirus
explanation: No scientific evidence supports the claim that cow urine prevents or treats COVID-19. Health authorities and researchers have repeatedly rejected this claim. Relying on unproven remedies may delay proper medical care.

claim: Adding pepper to food prevents coronavirus infection
explanation: Adding pepper to food does not prevent coronavirus infection. Hot peppers and spices may enhance flavor but are not COVID-19 treatments. Proven preventive measures include vaccination, hand hygiene, and avoiding exposure to infection.

myth: Alkaline water changes body pH and cures disease
claim: Drinking alkaline water can change body pH and cure diseases
explanation: The body tightly regulates blood pH through the lungs and kidneys. Drinking alkaline water does not significantly alter blood pH in healthy individuals. There is currently insufficient high-quality evidence proving that alkaline water cures diseases.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Eating sugar directly causes diabetes
explanation: Type 2 diabetes develops from a combination of genetic, lifestyle, and environmental factors. Excess sugar intake can contribute to obesity, which is a major risk factor. Sugar alone has not been established as the sole direct cause of diabetes.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Eating after 8 PM causes weight gain
claim: Eating late at night causes weight gain
explanation: Weight gain is mainly influenced by total calorie intake and energy expenditure. Eating late does not automatically result in weight gain. Scientific evidence remains mixed regarding meal timing and body weight.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Honey is always healthier than sugar
claim: Honey is always a healthier alternative to sugar
explanation: Honey contains small amounts of antioxidants and micronutrients. Both honey and sugar can increase blood glucose levels. Evidence does not conclusively establish honey as universally healthier than sugar for all individuals.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Coconut oil can cure Alzheimer's disease
explanation: Some early studies explored potential benefits of medium-chain fatty acids on cognition. Existing research is insufficient to establish coconut oil as a treatment or cure. Major health authorities do not recommend coconut oil for treating Alzheimer's disease.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Apple cider vinegar melts body fat
claim: Apple cider vinegar can melt body fat
explanation: Some studies suggest small effects on appetite and blood sugar management. There is no strong evidence that apple cider vinegar alone causes significant fat loss. Sustainable weight loss generally requires long-term dietary and lifestyle changes.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Charcoal drinks can detox the body
explanation: Activated charcoal is used medically for selected poisoning cases. Evidence does not clearly support routine use of charcoal drinks for detoxification. Regular consumption may interfere with nutrient and medication absorption.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Gluten-free diets are healthier for everyone
claim: Gluten-free diets are healthier for everyone
explanation: Gluten-free diets are medically necessary for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity. Healthy individuals may not experience additional benefits from avoiding gluten. More evidence is needed before recommending gluten-free diets universally.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Superfoods can prevent all diseases
explanation: Certain foods contain beneficial nutrients and antioxidants. No single food has been proven to prevent all diseases. Long-term health depends on overall lifestyle, nutrition, and genetics rather than one food source.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Cracking knuckles causes arthritis
explanation: Research has not established a connection between knuckle cracking and arthritis. The cracking sound is caused by gas bubbles within joint fluid. Habitual knuckle cracking is generally not associated with joint damage.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Reading in dim light permanently damages eyesight
claim: Reading in dim light causes permanent eye damage
explanation: Reading in dim light may cause temporary eye strain or discomfort. Vision usually returns to normal after resting the eyes. There is no clear evidence that reading in low light causes permanent eye damage.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Cold weather directly causes colds
explanation: Colds are caused by viruses rather than cold temperatures alone. People tend to spend more time indoors during colder weather, increasing exposure to respiratory viruses. Exposure to cold weather by itself does not directly cause a viral infection.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Hair and nails continue growing after death
claim: Hair and nails grow after death
explanation: Hair and nails do not actually continue to grow after death. Dehydration causes the skin to shrink, creating the appearance of growth. Cell growth processes stop after death.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Mobile phone use causes brain cancer
explanation: Research has not established a definitive causal relationship between mobile phone use and brain cancer. Large studies have not consistently shown increased cancer risk at normal exposure levels. Scientific monitoring and research continue to evaluate long-term effects.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Microwave cooking makes food radioactive
explanation: Microwave ovens use non-ionizing radiation to heat food. Food heated in a microwave does not become radioactive. When used according to manufacturer instructions, microwave cooking is generally considered safe.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Sitting too close to TV ruins eyesight
claim: Sitting close to TV causes permanent eyesight damage
explanation: Sitting close to a television may cause temporary eye strain or discomfort. It does not necessarily result in permanent eyesight damage. Consistently sitting very close to a screen may indicate an existing vision issue that should be evaluated.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: You must drink exactly 8 glasses of water daily
claim: Everyone must drink exactly 8 glasses of water per day
explanation: Hydration needs vary based on age, body size, activity level, health status, and climate. Fluids can come from beverages as well as foods. There is no universal requirement that everyone must drink exactly eight glasses of water per day.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Daily vitamin supplements are necessary for everyone
explanation: Many people obtain essential nutrients through a balanced diet. Some individuals may require supplements because of medical conditions, age, pregnancy, or deficiencies. Daily supplementation is not universally necessary for every person.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Sweating removes toxins from the body
explanation: Sweating primarily helps regulate body temperature. The liver and kidneys perform most of the body's detoxification processes. Sweat contains only small amounts of waste products and is not the body's primary detox mechanism.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Diabetes can be permanently cured with herbal remedies
claim: Herbal remedies can permanently cure diabetes
explanation: Some herbs may influence blood sugar levels, but evidence varies considerably. No herbal remedy has been scientifically proven to permanently cure diabetes. Diabetes requires ongoing monitoring and evidence-based medical management.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Insulin use causes kidney failure
explanation: Kidney damage is a common complication of uncontrolled diabetes. Insulin is used to help manage blood glucose levels and reduce complications associated with diabetes. There is no established evidence showing that insulin directly causes kidney failure.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Blood pressure medicine should be stopped once BP is normal
claim: Blood pressure medication can be stopped when BP is normal
explanation: Blood pressure may remain normal because the medication is working effectively. Stopping medication without medical advice may cause blood pressure to rise again. Any changes to treatment should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Biopsies cause cancer to spread
explanation: Biopsies are commonly used to diagnose and evaluate suspected cancers. Modern biopsy procedures are designed to minimize risks and are routinely performed worldwide. There is no conclusive evidence supporting the claim that biopsies generally cause cancer to spread.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

claim: Natural products are always safe to use
explanation: Natural substances can have side effects, interactions, or toxic effects. Some herbal and natural products may interfere with prescription medications. Safety depends on the product, dosage, quality, and the individual's health condition.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Antibiotics should be stopped when you feel better
claim: Antibiotics can be stopped once symptoms improve
explanation: Antibiotic treatment should be used according to healthcare provider instructions. Stopping medication prematurely may affect treatment outcomes in certain situations. Responsible antibiotic use is important to help reduce antimicrobial resistance.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Stress is always bad for health
claim: Stress is always harmful to health
explanation: Stress can affect people differently depending on its duration and intensity. Short-term stress may help improve focus or performance in certain situations. Long-term unmanaged stress may have negative effects on physical and mental well-being.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Mental illness is a sign of weakness
claim: Mental illness indicates personal weakness
explanation: Mental health conditions are influenced by biological, psychological, and environmental factors. Mental illnesses can affect people from all walks of life. Seeking professional help is an important part of managing mental health concerns.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.

myth: Sleeping less than 5 hours is fine if you feel okay
claim: Sleeping less than 5 hours is acceptable if you feel fine
explanation: Sleep needs vary among individuals, but adequate sleep is generally important for overall health. Some people may underestimate the effects of chronic sleep deprivation. Long-term lack of sleep has been associated with various health concerns and reduced performance.
note: There is no evidence for this claim, hence request to consult a healthcare professional.
